analysis.one_liner: Forced tobacco companies to fund public health and cut teen smoking while shielding them from most future lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 1997 with 2 Republican cosponsors and heard by the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 1998, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never brought to a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a comprehensive attempt to settle the tobacco wars. Cigarette makers would have paid roughly $10 billion up front and about $500 billion over 25 years into a trust fund for states, public health programs, NIH research, and tobacco farmer buyouts. In exchange, they would gain sweeping protections against lawsuits: pending state and class actions terminated, punitive damages for past conduct barred, and future class actions banned. The bill also gave the government new power to regulate tobacco as a health product, banned most tobacco advertising, set mandatory targets for cutting teen smoking, and dissolved the Tobacco Institute.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would be young people (mandatory reductions in underage tobacco use backed by financial penalties on manufacturers), states (reimbursement for tobacco-related health costs and block grants), NIH-funded researchers, victims of asbestos linked to smoking, and tobacco farm families receiving buyout payments. Tobacco manufacturers would also have benefited substantially, gaining certainty and near-immunity from the wave of lawsuits then pending against them.

how_it_helps.text: Sets national goals to cut teen cigarette use 30% by year five, 50% by years seven through nine, and 60% by year ten, with surcharges on manufacturers if the targets are missed.

Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services power to set tobacco health-risk standards, limit tar, require ingredient disclosure, and regulate nicotine, amending the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to cover tobacco.

Requires $10 billion in upfront licensing fees plus roughly $16.5 billion per year for 25 years, split between reimbursing states for tobacco-related health costs, public health and anti-smoking programs, NIH research, asbestos victims, and a tobacco farmer transition.

Bans outdoor tobacco advertising, cartoon and human-image advertising, product placement in movies and video games, event sponsorships, and branded merchandise, and forces termination of the Tobacco Institute and Council for Tobacco Research.
Requires a public depository of internal tobacco company documents on smoking and health and restricts tobacco industry lobbying.
Provides buyout and transition payments to tobacco quota owners, producers, and workers as the price support program is phased out.

analysis.who_pays: Adult smokers would pay through higher cigarette prices, since the bill explicitly allows manufacturers to pass fee costs through to consumers, and price-driven taxes fall hardest on lower-income smokers. Sick smokers and their families would give up legal remedies: class actions terminated, punitive damages for pre-enactment conduct barred, and damage payments subject to an annual aggregate cap. Plaintiffs' attorneys would lose the contingent-fee litigation that had produced the state settlements.

drawbacks.text: Grants sweeping liability protections to participating manufacturers: pending health-related suits by states and pending class actions are terminated, punitive damages for past conduct are barred, and new class actions are banned.

Sets an annual aggregate limit on judgment and settlement payments and gives manufacturers a credit for 80% of payments made against their fees, which could leave injured smokers uncompensated in heavy judgment years.

The bill's own findings state the industry 'concealed relevant data concerning the effects of tobacco products,' yet it would shield that conduct from punitive damages — the trade-off critics on both sides seized on.
Allows manufacturers to pass the settlement costs through to prices, meaning the burden lands on consumers, disproportionately lower-income smokers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On public health terms the bill was aggressive: binding youth-reduction targets, FDA-style regulation, an advertising near-ban, and hundreds of billions directed to states and public health, all funded by industry. The price was a negotiated peace that would have stripped courts of the power to punish the industry's past conduct and capped its exposure — worth enormous sums to manufacturers at the moment they faced potentially ruinous litigation. An honest supporter had to concede the liability shield was the industry's half of the bargain, and that fee costs would reach consumers through prices. Whether that trade was worth it was the core dispute; the Senate never resolved it, because the bill never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, heard by the Judiciary Committee, and placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced S. 1530 on November 13, 1997.
It was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 298) on January 27, 1998.
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on the bill on February 10, 1998 (printed as S.Hrg. 105-541).
No further action was taken; the bill received no Senate floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided the bill's roughly $500 billion in fees, its advertising bans, and its youth-reduction mandates, while the public received none of the promised health programs or FDA tobacco authority. States went on to negotiate their own 1998 settlement without the federal liability shield this bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cigarette makers facing no new rules

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Sponsored S. 1530 and held Judiciary Committee hearings on it in February 1998.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 1530 or any comprehensive tobacco settlement bill to a final Senate vote in 1998; the Senate's only floor action on settlement legislation was a June 1998 vote to cut off debate on a rival bill that fell short of the 60 votes needed.

against.name: Tobacco product manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Ran advertising and lobbying campaigns against comprehensive tobacco settlement legislation in 1998; the bill would have imposed about $500 billion in fees, banned most of their marketing, and dissolved the Tobacco Institute.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call was ever taken on this bill; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, while the broader 1998 Senate fight over tobacco settlement legislation split both parties — the only settlement bill to reach the floor failed a procedural vote 57-43, with members of each party on both sides.

industries.note: The bill would have taken about $500 billion from manufacturers over 25 years, imposed strict product and marketing regulation, and dissolved the Tobacco Institute — but in exchange it locked in tobacco's legal status, granted near-immunity from government and class-action suits, barred punitive damages for past conduct, and capped annual damage payments. The shield's cost falls on sick smokers and state treasuries, while the fees would reach consumers through prices.

Pending class actions would be terminated, punitive damages barred, and attorneys' fees capped at 5% of annual fees and awarded only through an arbitration panel. Their loss mirrors smokers' loss of collective legal remedies.

The bill provides buyout and transition payments to owners, producers, and displaced workers, plus rural block grants, as the quota and price support programs are ended — compensation for families affected by a public health policy.

industries.industry: Advertising, media, and event sponsorship businesses
industries.note: Outdoor advertising, cartoon and human-image ads, product placement in film and video games, branded merchandise, and event sponsorships would all be banned, removing a major advertising category. The loss serves the bill's youth-protection goal.
